Longbill spearfish (Tetrapturus pfluegeri) exhibit a life history shaped by the warm, pelagic waters of the Atlantic. Based on comparative data from the closely related striped marlin (Kajikia audax) at a consistent water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the incubation period for this species is estimated to be approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], reflecting the rapid developmental rates common among tropical billfishes. The newly hatched lecithotrophic larva emerges from a buoyant, yolk-laden egg with an initial wet weight of just 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], derived from an assumed egg diameter of one millimeter. This minute mass, characteristic of pelagic teleost larvae, underscores the extreme vulnerability of the early life stages to starvation and predation before the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva, still reliant on endogenous reserves, must quickly complete the transition to active foraging in the planktonic environment.

As individuals progress through the exotrophic larval phase and into the juvenile stage, somatic growth proceeds at an accelerated pace. The species attains a total length of 150 centimeters [Lp = 150 centimeters] at the point of sexual maturation, a value that represents the length at puberty. This size is considerably smaller than the ultimate total length the species is capable of achieving, indicating a prolonged period of post-maturation growth that is typical among iteroparous billfishes. Females in particular benefit from this continued expansion because fecundity in teleosts scales positively with body size. Reaching this pubertal length involves a multi-year trajectory during which the growing juvenile must navigate the energetic demands of migration and feeding in the open ocean before investing resources into gonad development.

Reproductive output in Tetrapturus pfluegeri is considerable, reflecting its position as a highly fecund pelagic spawner. When a female reaches a fork length of approximately 277 centimeters, her daily reproductive rate is estimated at roughly 79,452 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 79,452 eggs per day], a figure derived from studies of the congeneric Kajikia audax under the stable thermal regime of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C]. This high daily reproductive output is achieved through the production of numerous batches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning season. The estimate assumes that spawning occurs on a nearly daily basis during the peak reproductive window, a strategy that disperses offspring across a wide spatial area. Such a high fecundity compensates for the exceptionally low survival rates experienced by the planktonic eggs and early larvae in the oligotrophic marine environment.

The timing of major life history transitions in the longbill spearfish is tightly linked to thermal conditions. Researchers, using growth increment data obtained at 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], have estimated that first reproduction occurs at approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching]. This two-year interval to first spawning is relatively rapid for a large istiophorid and suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes early breeding. The age at first reproduction is consistent with the total length at puberty of 150 centimeters [Lp = 150 centimeters], as growth rates during the juvenile phase are sufficient to attain this length within the two-year window under favorable oceanographic conditions, such as those encountered in the central Atlantic.

Maximum recorded longevity for Tetrapturus pfluegeri, again based on otolith increment analyses conducted at a thermal baseline of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], is estimated to be around 10 years [am = around 10 years]. This lifespan, while moderate compared to some long-lived teleosts, allows for multiple reproductive cycles and substantial terminal body size attainment. The ultimate wet weight associated with the longest-lived and largest individuals is approximately 58,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 58,000 grams], representing the maximum published body mass for the species. Interestingly, an allometric calculation based on the ultimate total length of 254 centimeters [Li = 254 centimeters] yields a higher theoretical value of around 159,000 grams, suggesting that the observed maximum weight may be constrained by ecological factors such as prey availability or fishing mortality rather than by physiological limits alone. This discrepancy highlights the value of empirical records in defining life history parameters.
